mainTopic: When does a thief own a stolen item? שינוי השם (the beam, the water duct, הקדש and תרומה), the פסוק source for שינוי קונה, and עולא on יאוש
overview: This amud asks when a thief becomes the owner of what he stole. It starts with a stolen beam built into a building. The ruling there needs תקנת השבים to let the thief pay instead of returning the beam, which suggests the name change alone did not count. רב יוסף answers that a beam keeps its name even inside a house, and he proves it from a ברייתא on a פסוק in יחזקאל. רבי זירא answers instead that a name change which can undo itself does not count. The גמרא then tests whether a lasting name change counts, using a log hollowed into a water duct for a מקוה. It defends the rule by noting that drawn water is only a rabbinic law and that the log was never a כלי while detached. A ברייתא saying a thief's הקדש, תרומה and מעשר are valid is explained by the name change those acts create. Next come two opposite versions of רב חסדא in the name of רבי יונתן on whether the פסוק "והשיב את הגזילה אשר גזל" teaches that a change makes the thief the owner. Finally, עולא begins to prove from מלאכי that יאוש alone does not give the thief ownership, and his proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Without the special rule, the beam would go back as is
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the ברייתא about the stolen beam closely. It concludes that if not for תקנת השבים, the beam would have to be returned as is, even though its name seems to have changed.
steps.simpleTranslation: This implies that if not for this (the special rule), the beam would be returned as it is!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes a close reading of the ruling about a stolen מריש built into a building. It points out that the ruling only lets the thief pay money because of תקנת השבים, so otherwise the beam itself would go back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a name change counted as a real change, the thief would own the beam anyway and would not need a special rule. Since the ברייתא needs תקנת השבים, it seems the name change does not count. That is a problem for anyone who holds that שינוי השם is a real change.

keyTerms.meaning: But if not for this: it marks an inference from what the source says.
It goes back as it is: the actual item is returned, not money.
A wooden beam.
The rabbinic rule made so that thieves can repent easily.

phrases.english: But if not for this,
phrases.notes: "This" is the special rule for people who want to repent, letting the thief pay money instead of tearing down the building.

phrases.english: it would go back as it is!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion about whether שינוי השם counts as a change, using the case of the beam built into a building.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a change of name (שינוי השם) counts as a real change.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא needs תקנת השבים to let the thief keep the beam. So without that rule, the beam would go back despite its name change, which means the name change did not transfer ownership.

steps.title: רב יוסף: a beam keeps its name
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that there was no real name change at all. A מריש is still called a מריש even after it is built into a house.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: a beam keeps its name on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the challenge by denying that the beam's name ever changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that building the beam in changed its name. רב יוסף says it did not, so this case says nothing about whether a real name change counts. The view that שינוי השם is a change is safe.

keyTerms.meaning: Its name is still on it: it keeps its original name.
A change of name: when an item comes to be called something new.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
a beam keeps its name on it,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: מָרִישׁ – שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: there was never a name change here.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought a beam built into a house gets a new name, so the case would prove that a name change does not count.
steps.terutzMaskana: A beam is still called מריש inside the building, so the case is not about a name change at all.

steps.title: Proof from a פסוק: beams inside a house are still called מרישות
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains the words of a פסוק in יחזקאל. It identifies the עובים as beams, which shows that beams built into a house are still called מרישות.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'צלעות הבית': these are the casings. 'והעבים': these are the beams.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רב יוסף. It shows that wood already built into a house is still called מרישות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes parts of a finished building. The ברייתא calls those parts מרישות, so the name 'beam' stays even after building. That supports רב יוסף's claim that nothing changed.

keyTerms.meaning: The sides of the house: a phrase from the פסוק.
Casings or panels.
A word from the פסוק that the ברייתא explains as beams.

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'The tzalot of the house': these are the casings,
'And the ubbim': these are the beams.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב יוסף's answer in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That a beam keeps the name מריש even after it is built into a house.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא explaining 'וְהָעֻבִּים' in יחזקאל 41:26 as מרישות.

steps.title: רבי זירא: a name change that can undo itself does not count
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא gives a different answer. Even if the name did change, a name change where the item can go back to its first form is not a real change.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: a change that can go back to its original state, when it comes to a change of name, is not a change.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא gives a second answer to the challenge from step 1. He grants that the name may change, but says this kind of name change does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The beam can be pulled out of the building and become a plain beam again. Since the change can undo itself, it does not count as a real change. So the case does not prove that a permanent name change fails to count.

keyTerms.meaning: A change that can go back to its original state.
It is not a change: it does not count as a change in הלכה.

steps.confusionAlert: רבי זירא does not argue that the beam's name stays the same, as רב יוסף did. He accepts a name change and limits which name changes count.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
a change that goes back to its original state,
in a change of name, is not a change.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the same challenge that רב יוסף answered.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the rule: only a name change that cannot be reversed counts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any name change, including the beam's, would count as a change.
steps.terutzMaskana: A name change that can reverse, like a beam that can be removed, does not count. So the case says nothing about permanent name changes.

steps.title: Does a permanent name change count? The case of the water duct
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether even a permanent name change counts. It brings the case of a log hollowed into a duct, which has a new name, together with a ברייתא about how such a duct affects a מקוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does a change of name that does not go back to its original state count as a change? But there is the duct, which at first was called a log and now is called a duct. And it was taught: a duct that one hollowed out and then attached disqualifies the מקוה. If one attached it and then hollowed it out, it does not disqualify the מקוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges whether a permanent name change counts as a change. It lays out the case of the duct and a ברייתא about the מקוה. This step sets up the challenge, and the conclusion drawn from it comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A log hollowed into a duct gets a new name and cannot turn back into a log, so it is a permanent name change. The ברייתא says the order matters: hollowed first and then attached disqualifies the מקוה, but attached first and then hollowed does not. The גמרא is about to use this ruling to test whether the new name really makes a difference.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it really? It opens a doubtful challenge.
A duct or pipe for carrying water.
A cut log.
He hollowed it out.
He fixed it in place: attached it to the ground or a building.
Disqualifies the ritual bath.

steps.confusionAlert: Order is everything in the ברייתא. Hollowed and then attached disqualifies the מקוה. Attached and then hollowed does not.

phrases.english: And a change of name that does not go back to its original state,
is it a change?
But there is the duct,
which at first was called 'a log',
and now is called 'a duct',
and it was taught: a duct that one hollowed out
and afterward attached,
disqualifies the ritual bath.
phrases.notes: Hollowed first, it counts as a vessel, and water that passes through a vessel can't fill a מקוה.

phrases.english: If one attached it and afterward hollowed it out,
it does not disqualify the ritual bath.
phrases.notes: Once attached, the log is part of the ground, so hollowing it there never makes it a vessel.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשִׁינּוּי הַשֵּׁם שֶׁאֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר לִבְרִיָּיתוֹ, מִי הָוֵי שִׁינּוּי? וַהֲרֵי צִינּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רבי זירא's distinction and questions whether even a permanent name change counts as a change.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that a permanent name change (שינוי השם שאינו חוזר לבריתו) counts as a real change.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The duct is a clear case of a permanent name change, from log to duct. The ברייתא about the מקוה gives a ruling on it, and the גמרא is about to use that ruling to test whether the new name really changes anything.

steps.title: If a name change matters, the attached-then-hollowed log should also disqualify
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the question from step 5: if a new name counts as a real change, then even a log attached first and hollowed later should invalidate the מקוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that a change of name is significant, then even if he attached the log first and only afterward hollowed it out, it should also disqualify the מקוה!
steps.whatsHappening: This is the punchline of the question that was set up in step 5. The גמרא points to the second case of the ברייתא, where the מקוה stays valid, and asks why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In that case the log became a 'duct' with a new name only after it was attached to the ground. If a new name makes it a new item, it should now count as a כלי, and water flowing through a כלי is drawn water that ruins a מקוה. Since the ברייתא says the מקוה is valid there, it seems a name change does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say: it introduces the result of accepting a view.
It is something significant; it counts
It should disqualify (the מקוה)

phrases.english: And if you say
that a change of name is significant,
then even if he attached it and afterward hollowed it out
phrases.notes: This is the second case of the ברייתא from step 5, where the מקוה is ruled valid.

phrases.english: it should also disqualify!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ שִׁינּוּי הַשֵּׁם מִילְּתָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge that step 5 set up with the hollowed-log ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a name change, even a permanent one, counts as a real change.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא treats a log hollowed after it was attached as not a כלי, even though it now has a new name. So a name change does not seem to create a new item.

steps.title: Drawn water is only a rabbinic rule, so there is room to be lenient
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the rule disqualifying a מקוה with drawn water is מדרבנן, so the חכמים were lenient in that case.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case of drawn water is different, because that rule is מדרבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the view that a name change counts. The מקוה case is different because the law of שאיבה is only rabbinic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A name change may really count, and the hollowed log may really be a new item. But since the problem of drawn water is only מדרבנן, the חכמים chose not to disqualify the מקוה in that case. So the ברייתא tells us nothing about name changes in general.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different
Drawn water, meaning water that came through a כלי and so cannot fill a מקוה
Rabbinic law, not from the Torah

phrases.english: Drawn water is different,
because it is only rabbinic.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the leniency comes from the rabbinic nature of שאיבה, not from the name change failing to count.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The valid מקוה proves a name change does not create a new item.
steps.terutzMaskana: A name change may count. The מקוה stays valid only because the rule of drawn water is מדרבנן.

steps.title: Then the first case should be lenient too
steps.stepSummary: If the leniency comes from שאיבה being rabbinic, the first case of the ברייתא, where the log was hollowed first and then attached, should also be valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then even in the first case it should also be valid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer of step 7. The same reason should also apply to the first case of the ברייתא, yet there the מקוה is disqualified.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says a log hollowed first and attached later does disqualify the מקוה. If 'it is only rabbinic' were enough of a reason to be lenient, that case should be valid too. So step 7 seems to prove too much.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
The first case (literally, the head) of a teaching

phrases.english: If so,
then even the first case as well!
phrases.notes: The first case is where he hollowed the log first and attached it afterward. There the ברייתא says the מקוה is disqualified.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the rabbinic nature of שאיבה explains the leniency.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reason applies equally to the first case, yet the ברייתא is strict there.

steps.title: A log that was a vessel while detached is different
steps.stepSummary: In the first case the log was already a כלי while it was detached from the ground. In the second case it never was a כלי while detached, so the חכמים were lenient there.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it had the status of a כלי while it was detached. Here, it never had the status of a כלי while detached.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the two cases of the ברייתא are treated differently, even though both involve a rabbinic rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A log hollowed before it was attached was a full כלי, so it stays a כלי even after it is attached, and the מקוה is disqualified. A log hollowed only after it was attached was never a detached כלי. Its new status comes only from the name change, and for a rabbinic rule the חכמים did not treat that as enough.

keyTerms.meaning: The status of a vessel
Detached (not attached to the ground)
There / here: used to contrast two cases

steps.whatToRemember: The hollowed-log case does not disprove שינוי השם. The מקוה is valid only because שאיבה is מדרבנן and the log never was a כלי while detached.

phrases.english: There, it has the status of a vessel
while detached,
here, it does not have the status of a vessel
while detached.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם אִיכָּא תּוֹרַת כְּלִי עָלָיו בְּתָלוּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 by pointing out a real difference between the two cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the two cases of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the rabbinic nature of שאיבה brings leniency, it should do so in both cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leniency applies only where the log never was a כלי while detached.

steps.title: A thief's הקדש, תרומה and מעשר are valid
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a גנב, גזלן, or אנס can make the items he took into valid הקדש, תרומה, and מעשר. This seems to show he owns them even without any change in the item.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this: A thief, a robber, and one who forces a sale: their הקדש is הקדש, their תרומה is תרומה, and their מעשר is מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge from a ברייתא. It attacks the view that a thief does not own the stolen item until it has been changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the owner can make an item הקדש or separate תרומה and מעשר from it. If the thief's acts take effect, he must already own the item. Nothing physical happened to it, so the item seems to be his with no change at all, perhaps just through the owner's יאוש.

keyTerms.meaning: A thief who takes secretly / a robber who takes openly
One who forces the owner to sell to him
Property set aside for the בית המקדש
Gifts that must be separated from produce

phrases.english: They challenged:
A thief, a robber, and one who forces a sale:
their consecration is valid consecration,
and their תרומה is valid תרומה,
and their tithes are valid tithes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the hollowed-log discussion ends, the גמרא brings a new challenge on the larger question of when a thief owns the stolen item.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a thief does not own the stolen item without some change.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only an owner can make הקדש or separate תרומה and מעשר. The thief's acts work even though the item is unchanged, so he must own it already.

steps.title: The act itself creates a name change
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that in those cases there is a name change: טבל becomes תרומה, and חולין becomes הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: There, there is a change of name. At first it was called טבל and now it is called תרומה. With הקדש, at first it was called חולין and now it is called הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of step 10. The thief's own act gives the item a new name, and that change is what lets his act work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא does not prove that a thief owns an unchanged item. Separating תרומה turns the produce from 'טבל' into 'תרומה', and consecrating it turns 'חולין' into 'הקדש'. Since a name change counts as a real change, these cases fit the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: טבל: produce from which תרומה and מעשר have not yet been taken
Ordinary, non-holy property

steps.whatToRemember: A thief's הקדש, תרומה, and מעשר work because the act itself creates a שינוי השם. This fits the view that a name change counts as a real change.

phrases.english: They say:
There, there is a change of name:
for at first it was 'untithed produce'
and now it is 'תרומה',
with consecration, at first it was 'non-sacred'
and now it is 'consecrated'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 using the idea that a name change counts.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the case: the act creates the change that gives the thief ownership.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The thief owns the item with no change at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The act of making הקדש or separating תרומה and מעשר is itself a שינוי השם, which counts as a real change.

steps.title: A פסוק source that a change lets the thief own the item
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא in the name of רבי יונתן learns from the extra words "אשר גזל" that a שינוי makes the stolen item belong to the thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רבי יונתן: How do we know that a change lets the thief own the item? The פסוק says "he shall return the stolen item that he stole." Why add "that he stole"? If the item is still the way it was when he stole it, he gives it back. If not, he just pays its value.
steps.whatsHappening: After the earlier questions about whether a שינוי makes the item belong to the thief, the גמרא now brings a פסוק that teaches it does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "אשר גזל" seem extra, so רבי יונתן reads them as a limit. Only when the item is still "like what he stole" must he return it. Once it has changed, he owes money instead, and the item itself stays with him.

keyTerms.meaning: A change in the stolen item
Acquires; becomes the owner
Why does the פסוק need to say this? (the words seem extra)
In the same state as when he stole it
Money; the value of the item

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Rabbi Yonatan said:
From where do we know that a change makes him the owner?
As it says: "And he shall return the stolen item"
Why does the verse add "that he stole"?
If it is like when he stole it, he returns it;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו – דָּמִים בְּעָלְמָא בָּעֵי שַׁלּוֹמֵי.
phrases.english: and if not, he only needs to pay money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the case-based discussion to a direct פסוק source for שינוי קונה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שינוי makes the stolen item belong to the thief, and he pays its value instead. This is learned from the extra words "אשר גזל".

steps.title: Those words are needed for a different law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that "אשר גזל" is needed to teach that a son does not add חומש when returning what his father stole.
steps.simpleTranslation: But these words "that he stole" are needed to leave out something his father stole. He does not add a fifth on his father's theft!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the source from step 12. It says the words "אשר גזל" are already being used for another law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thief who swore falsely must add a חומש (an extra fifth) when he pays back. "אשר גזל" (what *he* stole) limits this to the thief himself and not his heir. If the words teach that, they cannot also be used as a source for שינוי.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed (for another purpose)
To exclude
The extra fifth a thief who swore falsely must add
Something his father stole

phrases.aramaic: הַאי ״אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל״ מִיבְּעֵי לְמַעוֹטֵי גֶּזֶל אָבִיו,
phrases.english: But this "that he stole" is needed to exclude his father's theft,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵינוֹ מוֹסִיף חוֹמֶשׁ עַל גֶּזֶל אָבִיו!
phrases.english: that he does not add a fifth on his father's theft!
phrases.notes: The פסוק is talking about a thief who also swore falsely, and he pays an extra fifth.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי ״אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל״ מִיבְּעֵי לְמַעוֹטֵי גֶּזֶל אָבִיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source used in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using "אשר גזל" as the source that שינוי קונה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words are already used up teaching that an heir does not add חומש. So they are not free to teach something else.

steps.title: The wording teaches both laws
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah only meant the חומש law, it could have written "גזילו". The longer wording shows that both laws are learned.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the Torah should have written "and he shall return his stolen item." Why write "that he stole"? Learn two things from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 13. The Torah's choice of words is long enough to teach both laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The short word "גזילו" (his stolen item) would already show that the law is only about the thief himself. That alone covers the חומש law. Writing the longer "אשר גזל" adds something more: the item must be "like what he stole." That is the שינוי law.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One (the Torah)
Why do I need this?
Learn two things from it

steps.whatToRemember: In the first version, "אשר גזל" teaches two laws. A son does not add חומש on his father's theft, and a שינוי makes the item belong to the thief.

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן, נִיכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא ״וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת גְּזֵילוֹ״,
phrases.english: If so, let the Torah write "and he shall return his stolen item";
why do I need it to write "that he stole"?
Learn two things from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by showing the wording is long enough for both laws.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording: the longer phrase is more than one law needs.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The words "אשר גזל" can only teach the חומש law.
steps.terutzMaskana: "גזילו" would have been enough for the חומש law, so the longer "אשר גזל" also teaches שינוי קונה.

steps.title: Second version: a change does not let him own it
steps.stepSummary: Some report the opposite teaching: "והשיב את הגזילה" means he returns the item in every case, so a שינוי does not make it his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב חסדא said in the name of רבי יונתן: How do we know that a change does not make the thief the owner? The פסוק says "and he shall return the stolen item". That means in every case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of רב חסדא's teaching. In this version רבי יונתן holds the opposite: a שינוי does not make the item belong to the thief.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the focus is on "והשיב את הגזילה". It says to return *the stolen item* without any limit. So even after a change, he must give back the item itself.

keyTerms.meaning: In every case

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new אמורא arguing. It is the same רב חסדא quoting רבי יונתן, just reported the opposite way.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Rabbi Yonatan said:
From where do we know that a change does not make him the owner?
As it says: "And he shall return the stolen item"
in every case.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite version of step 12's teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שינוי does not make the stolen item belong to the thief. He must return the item no matter what.

steps.title: But the פסוק says "אשר גזל"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that "אשר גזל" seems to limit returning the item to when it is unchanged.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: "that he stole"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second version. The same פסוק includes "אשר גזל", which seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, "אשר גזל" was the very source that a שינוי does make the item his. So how can the second version say he returns it in every case?

keyTerms.meaning: But it is written!

phrases.english: But it is written: "that he stole"!

steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that he returns the item in every case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: "אשר גזל" seems to require returning the item only if it is still like what he stole.

steps.title: "אשר גזל" is only for the חומש law
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, "אשר גזל" teaches only that a person adds חומש on his own theft and not on his father's.
steps.simpleTranslation: That phrase is needed for this: on his own theft he adds a fifth, but he does not add a fifth on his father's theft.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 16. In this version, "אשר גזל" is used up by the חומש law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version does not accept the argument from extra wording in step 14. So "אשר גזל" teaches only one thing: the חומש is paid only on his own theft. Nothing is left over to teach שינוי קונה.

keyTerms.meaning: Adds a fifth
His own theft

steps.whatToRemember: The two versions read the same פסוק in opposite ways. In version one, "אשר גזל" teaches both the חומש law and שינוי קונה. In version two, "אשר גזל" teaches only the חומש law, and "והשיב את הגזילה" teaches that a שינוי does not make the item his.

phrases.english: That is needed for this:
on his own theft he adds a fifth,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין מוֹסִיף חוֹמֶשׁ עַל גֶּזֶל אָבִיו.
phrases.english: and he does not add a fifth on his father's theft.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by giving "אשר גזל" a different job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different purpose: the phrase is used for another law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "אשר גזל" limits returning the item to when it is unchanged.
steps.terutzMaskana: "אשר גזל" only limits the חומש to his own theft. It says nothing about שינוי.

steps.title: עולא's source that giving up hope does not transfer ownership
steps.stepSummary: עולא asks for the source that יאוש does not let the thief acquire a stolen item. He quotes a פסוק in מלאכי that lists a stolen animal together with a lame animal. He begins to learn the law of the stolen animal from the law of the lame animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: How do we know that when the owner gives up hope, the thief still does not become the owner? Because the פסוק says, "And you have brought what was stolen, and the lame, and the sick." A stolen animal is like a lame one. Just as a lame animal can never be fixed at all...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with עולא's statement that יאוש alone does not give the thief ownership, and starts his proof from a פסוק. The comparison is not finished yet; the next lines will complete it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא learns from a פסוק that places גזול (a stolen animal) right next to פסח (a lame animal), so the two must be alike. A lame animal can never be made fit as a קרבן. עולא is building toward the idea that a stolen animal also stays unfit even after the owner's יאוש, which would show that יאוש does not make it the thief's.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner giving up hope of getting his item back
Acquires; makes it legally his
Something stolen
A lame animal, unfit as a קרבן
Similar to; compared with
A fix or remedy

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether יאוש alone transfers ownership is a central question in the laws of theft. Here עולא takes a clear position that it does not.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר עוּלָּא: מִנַּיִין לְיֵאוּשׁ שֶׁאֵינוֹ קוֹנֶה?
phrases.english: Ulla said: From where do we know that despair does not acquire?
phrases.notes: He means: when the owner gives up hope, that alone does not make the thief the owner.

phrases.english: As it says: "And you have brought the stolen,"
phrases.notes: מלאכי 1:13. The נביא is rebuking people for bringing bad animals as קרבנות.

phrases.english: "and the lame, and the sick"
the stolen animal is like the lame one:

phrases.aramaic: מָה פִּסֵּחַ דְּלֵית לֵיהּ תַּקַּנְתָּא כְּלָל,
phrases.english: just as a lame animal has no fix at all,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא: מִנַּיִין לְיֵאוּשׁ שֶׁאֵינוֹ קוֹנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the topic of שינוי (steps 15-17) to a new question about יאוש, brought by עולא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יאוש alone does not let a thief acquire the stolen item. This is learned from the comparison of גזול to פסח in מלאכי 1:13, and the comparison continues in the next lines.
